newsitem.title: CHINA: China says can only open capital markets gradually.
newsitem.headline: China says can only open capital markets gradually.

text.p: A senior Chinese banking official was quoted on Saturday as saying China's capital markets are still at a very primitive stage and will be opened up only gradually.

"China is a developing country with its capital markets still in a fledgling state and regulations are incomplete," Yin Jieyan, vice-president of the People's Bank of China, was quoted as saying by the China Securities newspaper.

"The markets' capacity for supervision and self-discipline is weak and investors' sense of risk is poor," he told a seminar in Beijing on Friday. "As a result, China can only open its capital markets steadily and gradually."
China is under pressure to open its financial markets wider, including allowing the local currency to become fully convertible, to help it gain admission to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
China has agreed to make the renminbi convertible under the current account by the end of this year but it has yet to settle a timetable to allow full convertibility.
Yin said that until the end of 1995, China had absorbed a total of $229.1 billion in foreign exchange since it embarked on its far-reaching economic reforms in 1979.
With foreign exchange reserves hitting a record of $98.8 billion by the end of October, China was fully capable of paying back foreign debts, Yin said.
Beijing actively seeks inflows of foreign funds, but treats the process with caution and is strengthening supervision, Yin said.

"The aim of the central bank is to protect the interest of investors while at the same time closely watching the risk of international capital inflows to prevent sharp movements of short-term money which could cause a financial crisis," Yin said.
Yin said that in the Ninth Five-year Plan period from 1996 to 2000, priority would be given to stability of both economic growth and the Chinese yuan.
Foreign funds should be guided into key economic sectors where they would be more effective, such as energy, transportation and major raw materials, he said.
Yin said Beijing was working towards unifying policy treatment for domestic and foreign firms and allowing foreign investors to be treated the same as locals. He gave no details.
